slides.title: Your Core Customer is the one decision that makes many others.
slides.headline: Your Core Customer is the one decision that makes many others.
slides.support: Most companies serve anyone who will pay. The result:
body: A mediocre product.
Special to no one.
Nothing sets you apart.
No idea when to say yes, and when to say no.
notes: The Core Customer is the foundation of the strategy. It simplifies everything after it.
Serve everyone and you specialize in nothing. The product is average for all of them, and you cannot differentiate.
The hard part is not finding the right customer. Most founders can point to them. The hard part is choosing one.
Choosing does not mean refusing everyone else. It means the Core Customer wins the trade-offs.

artwork.alt: Three neutral gray figures look toward a crowd of gray figures. One figure in the crowd is green, and one of the three gestures toward it.

slides.title: Choosing one changed the company
slides.headline: We served over 100 industries. Choosing one changed the company.

panels.heading: Anyone who needed a screen
panels.support: Over 100 industries in 110 countries. Average at everything.

panels.heading: K-12 schools in North America
panels.support: One buyer. The whole strategy built around them.

panels.heading: 20% net profit, 5 years running
panels.support: Up from break-even. Growth rose to 20% a year.

notes: Byron’s story from Rise Vision, a digital signage company.
The most important decision was who the company was building for and, equally, who it was not.
The company later sold at more than five times its recurring revenue.

slides.title: The Core Customer is the person who decides to buy.
slides.headline: The Core Customer is the person who decides to buy.

panels.heading: One individual
panels.support: The person who makes the buying decision.

panels.heading: Served at a profit
panels.support: We can meet their needs and make money.

panels.heading: Not a recommender
panels.support: Someone who can say no but not yes is not the Core Customer.

notes: Ask: is this the decision maker or a user? Is it our customer, or our channel’s customer?
The buyer is whoever makes the buying decision and keeps buying. That can be a distributor.
In a company with divisions, do the Core Customer for the root company.

slides.title: Core Customer example
slides.headline: Core Customer example
notes: The same subscription company as the Market Map example. Small businesses are 55% of its revenue.
Walk the page once. Start with who they are, then the ranked needs and benefits. End with the persona and their share of revenue and profit.
Need #1 is why QHAG priority #1 removes 2 days from activation.

artwork.alt: An example Core Customer for the subscription company. Core Customer: owner of a small business. Description: the owner of a business with 10 to 50 staff. They decide alone, pay by card, and want it working this month without an IT person. Prioritized needs. 1, up and running in days. 2, a cost they can predict. 3, a person to call when stuck. Prioritized benefits. 1, live in 5 days or fewer. 2, one flat monthly price. 3, a named contact for 90 days. Persona: Dana, owner of a 20-person business. Revenue 55%, profit 60%.

slides.title: Who should we analyze?
slides.headline: Who should we analyze?
slides.support: Name every customer you think matters. Do this before you look at the Market Map.
body: Then check the Market Map for a customer you missed.
Add any future customer the map shows.
notes: Ask the question before showing the map. The answers double-check the map.
Do not discount any customer the team names.

slides.title: Describe each customer you think matters.
slides.headline: Describe each customer you think matters.
slides.support: Work on your own first. For each customer, write:
body: Description: who makes the buying decision, and can we serve their needs at a profit? 50 words or fewer.
Core need: their primary reason for buying from us.
Benefits: the key benefits we offer to satisfy that need.
notes: Each person fills in their own column in private. Show your answers, then agree.
The worksheet calls the benefits drivers.
Allow about 15 minutes.

artwork.alt: The Core Customer page with names only. Three blocks are lit: Description, Prioritized Needs and Prioritized Benefits. Core Customer, Persona, and Revenue and Profit are dim.

slides.title: Choose one Core Customer.
slides.headline: Choose one Core Customer.
slides.support: Cluster everyone’s answers into possible customers. For each one:
body: Brainstorm 5 to 8 needs, then rank the top 3. Needs, not wants.
Rank the top 3 benefits you offer that meet those needs.
Note their share of revenue and profit.
Then compare the number one needs across the customers.
Choose the one you would keep if you could serve only one.
notes: If the number one needs all differ, the company is spread too thin.
Do not skip the ranking.
Settle differences with a decision, not a compromise.
A team that cannot choose today ranks its candidates. Choosing then becomes homework, with an owner and a date.
Expect a couple of rounds before it is right. Allow about 40 minutes.

artwork.alt: The Core Customer page with names only. Four blocks are lit: Core Customer, Prioritized Needs, Prioritized Benefits, and Revenue and Profit. Description and Persona are dim.

slides.title: Give your Core Customer a name and a face.
slides.headline: Give your Core Customer a name and a face.
slides.support: Then bring them into every meeting.
body: A first name.
A job title.
Their daily reality.
Last, record their share of revenue and profit.
notes: Test the persona: what are they doing on a Tuesday at 7 AM?
At Rise Vision the persona was Clay, a K-12 IT administrator.
Put the persona on every meeting agenda.

artwork.alt: Three neutral gray figures sit at a table. A portrait card of a green-outlined figure with a blank name tag stands on the table. The three turn toward it.

slides.title: Your Core Customer, on one page.
slides.headline: Your Core Customer, on one page.
notes: End on the finished page. Ask one leader to read the team’s own Core Customer aloud, top to bottom.
If a block is still open, give it an owner and a date.

slides.title: What does your Core Customer change?
slides.headline: What does your Core Customer change?
body: 3HAG: does each capability serve their three ranked needs?
KFFM: does a widget, a function or a critical number change?
1HAG and QHAG: does a priority change?
Marketing: does your message speak to this customer?
Would you turn away revenue that does not fit?
notes: Next, test the 3HAG and the 1HAG with these answers, then build the QHAG.
A StoryBrand BrandScript can help the team craft the message. It tells the company’s story with the customer as the hero and the company as the guide. It comes from the book Building a StoryBrand.
Homework: add the Core Customer to the War Room in Metronome.
